Fractures of the Cuboid Bone
 CORE

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand and differentiate types of cuboid fractures.
Be familiar with physical examination characteristics and diagnostic imaging modalities.
Implement appropriate treatment recommendations for specific fracture types.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Overview
Fractures of the cuboid are uncommon and often occur with injuries to other parts of
the foot. Avulsion fractures are the most common type of cuboid fracture and typically

occur at the calcaneocuboid joint; however, the bony avulsion usually occurs from the
calcaneus rather than the cuboid. Stress fractures are more rare. The nutcracker
fracture results from a forced abduction of the forefoot on the hindfoot with the fourth
and fifth metatarsals and calcaneus acting as a pincer to compress the cuboid
(Resources 1 and 2).
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Fractures of the cuboid are not common. One group noted a rate of 1.8 cuboid fractures
per 100,000 people in the United Kingdom. The increasing frequency over the last two
decades likely resulted from efforts to improve survival in head-on collisions. Fractures
of the cuboid may result from direct trauma or from ligamentous avulsion.1 Stress
fractures of the cuboid also occur but not as commonly as stress fractures of other tarsal
bones, most notably the navicular or calcaneus.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The cuboid has a complex shape that closely resembles a pyramid. It has articulations with the
fourth and fifth metatarsals distally, the calcaneus proximally, and the navicular and lateral
cuneiform medially.
The cuboid is the only bone in the foot that is involved in the Chopart and Lisfranc
(tarsometatarsal) joints.
The cuboid helps form and is a critical structure for the lateral column of the foot. Although
the cuboid does not actively participate in axial weight bearing, it does allow for appropriate
distribution of weight in the foot through its role in the lateral column.
A groove on the undersurface of the cuboid allows for passage of the peroneus longus on its
way to the plantar-medial foot.

Vascular Anatomy
The vascularity of the cuboid seldom is of clinical concern, dissimilar from some other tarsal
bones. It receives blood supply from the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Nutcracker Fracture

Nutcracker Fracture
The nutcracker fracture, which results from forced plantar flexion and abduction, is the
most notable form of cuboid fracture. It often occurs with other foot injuries, specifically
other midfoot fractures because of the relatively high energy required to fracture the
cuboid.
Stress Fractures

Stress Fractures
Cuboid stress fractures are important to keep in mind as a possible cause of lateral foot
pain; however, they consist of only approximately 1% or fewer of all stress fractures.
Similar to most stress fractures, they are thought to result from mechanical overload of
the bone itself. Foot position may be a predisposing factor; however, this is difficult to
study given the uncommon nature of these injuries.
Injury Classification

Injury Classification
Fenton et al published the largest series on cuboid fractures and classified them into one
of five types (Resource 2). Type 1 fractures are avulsion injuries and account for almost

9/3/26, 4:13 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000647
3/11

50% of all cuboid fractures. Type 2 fractures are extra-articular fractures not associated
with any shortening of the lateral column. These injuries account for 13% of cuboid
fractures and commonly are associated with an avulsion fracture of the fifth metatarsal.
Type 3 fractures are intra-articular without another associated injury; these injuries
account for 6% of cuboid fractures. Type 4 fractures have concomitant injury to the
tarsometatarsal complex and account for 18% of injuries. Type 5 fractures are divided
into type 5a and type 5b, with type 5a being fractures with lateral column shortening and
type 5b being fractures with medial and lateral column shortening. These injuries
account for 6% and 7% of cuboid fractures, respectively.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination

Patient History and Physical Examination
In general, patients with a cuboid fracture present with localized pain and swelling.
Because these injuries can occur in combination with other injuries in the foot, the pain
and swelling may be hard to localize. Surgeons should evaluate for associated midfoot
injuries, especially in patients with a high-energy mechanism of injury. In general,
patients with a stress fracture present with an insidious onset of pain over the cuboid
that is worsened by activity and relieved by rest.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
If an injury to the cuboid is clinically suspected, plain radiographs should be obtained. These
should include AP, lateral, and internal oblique views. The internal oblique view may be
especially useful for visualizing the entire cuboid and its articulations and for determining loss
of height.
Computed Tomography

CT can help fully characterize the fracture pattern. CT is particularly useful in determining
optimal approach and fixation strategies in patients with comminuted injuries.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is seldom warranted in the evaluation of acute, traumatic injuries; however, MRI is the
best diagnostic imaging modality if a stress fracture is suspected. In addition, MRI may be
useful in evaluating considerable midfoot ligamentous injuries.
Management
Avulsion Fractures (Type 1)

Avulsion Fractures (Type 1)
Isolated avulsion fractures of the cuboid rarely require any management. These injuries
may be accompanied by other injuries in the midfoot that may necessitate more
aggressive management. In such instances, the injury would be classified as a type 4
fracture.
Extra-articular Fractures (Type 2)
These injuries are nondisplaced and, by definition, not associated with deformity. Therefore,
they generally do not require aggressive management.
Intra-articular Fractures (Type 3)

Intra-articular Fractures (Type 3)
These injuries are very similar to type 2 injuries, except the fracture lines extend into the
calcaneocuboid joint, the metatarsal-cuboid joint, or both; however, the length of the
lateral column and articular congruity are maintained. Therefore, these injuries also can

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000647
5/11

be managed nonsurgically. For type 2 and type 3 injuries, open reduction and internal
fixation may be considered if earlier mobilization of the foot is desired.
Associated Tarsometatarsal Joint Complex Injury (Type 4)

Associated Tarsometatarsal Joint Complex Injury (Type 4)
These injuries may require open reduction and internal fixation if dislocation of the
metatarsal-cuboid articulations and any resultant shortening of the lateral column are
present. Dorsal dislocation of the metatarsals usually occurs with a shear fracture of the
dorsal distal cuboid. Reduction of the joints is necessary, with trans-articular wires or
external fixation to maintain reduction. Internal fixation may be necessary in the cuboid
if the dorsal fragment is sufficiently large. In either situation, if bone loss is present after
restoration of column length, then bone grafting the defect is appropriate.
Fracture with Associated Midtarsal Disruption (Type 5)

Fracture with Associated Midtarsal Disruption (Type 5)
From a treatment standpoint, type 5a and type 5b injuries frequently require open
reduction and internal fixation and external fixation (or both) to restore column length
(lateral or medial and lateral, respectively) and articular congruity. For type 5b injuries,
medial bridge plating can be used, with bridging external fixation laterally or with open
reduction internal fixation and bone grafting to maintain lateral column length.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning

Preoperative Planning

6/11

Appropriate imaging studies are necessary, including a three-view radiographic series of
the foot. A CT scan is recommended in patients with a comminuted fracture to
determine the most appropriate surgical approach, plan reduction techniques, plan
screw trajectory, and anticipate plate placement.
Patient Positioning

Patient Positioning
Patient positioning depends largely on associated injuries that may require access to the
medial aspect of the foot. Therefore, a true lateral decubitus position is rarely
considered. Instead, a sloppy lateral position or a bump under the hip to roll the leg
internally may be beneficial to allow access to the medial and lateral columns. A triangle
can be placed under the knee to allow for a more plantigrade position of the foot.
Surgical Approach
A lateral approach approximately between the extensor digitorum brevis and the peroneus
brevis generally allows access to the cuboid and for evaluation of the proximal and distal
joints.
Surgical Fracture Fixation

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Plate fixation often is used in these fractures given the need to restore and maintain
length. Bone grafting with structural graft may be helpful in achieving this purpose,
especially with increasing levels of comminution. External fixation can be used as an
adjunct to maintain lateral column length; however, lateral stiffness is a concern.

Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
A period of non–weight bearing is imperative, and many surgeons recommend cast or
splint immobilization in the immediate postoperative period. Periods of non–weight
bearing vary considerably and generally are not based on science, especially for these
rare injuries. Six weeks of non–weight bearing followed by progressive–weight bearing in
a controlled ankle motion boot for 4 to 6 weeks likely is sufficient in most patients. If an
external fixator is used, removal as soon as 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively should be
considered, depending on stability. Lateral column stiffness is a legitimate concern; an
equally practical concern is loosening of the external fixation construct. In the
experience of the author of this lesson, an external fixator on the foot for this purpose
may not last 4 weeks postoperatively because of loosening of the fixation pins from the
adjacent bone.
Complications/Outcomes

Complications/Outcomes
The sural nerve can be injured during the surgical management of cuboid fractures and
must be protected. The most distal motor insertion point of the deep peroneal nerve is
the extensor digitorum brevis, which must be protected.
Posttraumatic arthritis in the calcaneocuboid or metatarsal-cuboid articulation is a
concern with higher energy injuries. Arthritis between the metatarsals and the cuboid is
more problematic because fusing those joints is not well tolerated (preservation of
lateral column mobility is recommended).
Persistent instability of either joint complex postinjury is rarely reported.

Loss of lateral column length may lead to deformity and pain. Lateral column stiffness
can occur in patients with more severe injuries and those that require protracted
immobilization or external fixation. Mobilization should be initiated as early as possible
to minimize the risk of stiffness.
Cuboid fractures are rare injuries on which few studies have been published. Therefore,
outcome data are limited or nonexistent. In the limited data that have been reported,
mainly on patients with higher level injuries, outcomes generally appear to be good;
however, this finding is based on a limited cohort, and many patients were not pain-free
at final follow-up.2
